country.comment: The study examines urban, rural, and agricultural water pricing and water sector reforms in Ghana nationwide.
country.where_found: PDF p. 2, Title, Abstract, and Introduction; Figure 1, PDF p. 4

effect_estimate.comment: Descriptive historical-institutional and secondary administrative figures only; no inferential statistical model or numeric causal effect estimate is reported.
effect_estimate.value: Descriptive institutional-historical synthesis (no inferential statistical effect estimate reported): Statutory mandates requiring ministerial/government tariff approval (Act 310 of 1965; SMCD 85 of 1977) produced multi-year delays (1978 GWSC tariff proposal approved in 1981; 1982 proposal approved in 1984; 1980 GIDA proposal approved in 1984 and legalized by L.I. 1350 in 1987) so inflation rendered tariffs inadequate, while centralized rural tariffs recovered only about 10% of GWSC handpump maintenance costs. Low-income groups (over 60% of the population in rural, urban-fringe, and dense urban areas) had least water access, paying >10 times official rates to vendors and spending >10% of income on potable water. Following institutional and legal reforms—shifting tariff regulation to the independent PURC (Act 538 of 1997, approving 130% tariff increase in 1998, 30% in 1999, and 40% in 2002), establishing WRC (Act 522 of 1996) and autonomous CWSA with 5% community capital-cost contributions, and implementing the $240 million Water Sector Rehabilitation Project—33 urban systems (95% of GWSC production) were rehabilitated and Unaccounted For Water declined from 57% (1997) to 50% (1998), while CWSA operated in 82 of 110 districts and constructed 2,177 boreholes (101% achievement), 2,612 hand-dug wells (125%), 7,637 household latrines (103%), and 367 institutional/school latrines (87%). Reported urban coverage changed from 76% (1992) to 70% (1999) and rural/national coverage from 46% (1992) to 30% (1998), which the authors state are not comparable due to reclassifying and transferring small-town systems (populations up to 15,000) to District Assemblies.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF pp. 3–7, Experiences in Water Pricing, Difficulties or Problems, The Reform Process, and Achievements/Successes

mechanism_certainty.comment: Design ceiling for Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework is at most 2; rated 1 because the study synthesizes statutory provisions and descriptive secondary sector statistics rather than collecting primary empirical data directly observing household-level access transitions.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF pp. 2–8, History of Water Pricing in Ghana, Experiences in Water Pricing, The Reform Process, and Achievements/Successes

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines statutory tariff-setting, cost-recovery charges, subsidies, 2% urban cross-subsidy levy, and 5% rural community capital contributions (fees); multi-year ministerial tariff approval delays and slow repair responses (delay); sectoral vs. integrated water planning and District Assembly vs. urban utility service boundaries (planning, service_area); lack of inter-agency coordination and creation of WRC/PURC/CWSA (institutional_fragmentation, political_coordination); community WATSAN management, farmer cooperatives, and PURC public hearings (participation); CWSA facilitation/training (bureaucratic_assistance); and District Assembly budget support / vulnerable-group strategies for communities unable to pay (accommodation).
